kaigo-review-05-summary.heading: Today’s learning goals
paragraphs: Separate confirmed facts from assumptions and explain errors in your own words.
Check understanding with a new example and carry unfinished tasks into further learning.

kaigo-review-05-knowledge-0.heading: Distinguish error types
paragraphs: When checking answers, examine why an error occurred as well as the correct option number. Distinguishing gaps in understanding, misread subjects or times, missed conditions, assumptions beyond the evidence and unclear communication helps identify the next practice task.

Remembering an answer’s position does not necessarily show understanding. Identify confirmed facts and remaining unknowns, then check whether you can explain the same distinction in another situation.

kaigo-review-05-knowledge-1.heading: Practice one task with a new example
paragraphs: Today, choose one error type from the two submitted exercises. Check the necessary knowledge and sentence conditions, then create and explain another specific example. Do not treat every error as resolved at once; retain remaining tasks in the next plan.

Separate tasks requiring hand positioning, controlled force or coordination, such as transfers and personal cleaning, as practical training items. Reading a procedure and performing it safely are different achievements. Check practical skills through facility instruction and the individual care plan.

kaigo-review-05-knowledge-2.heading: Separate study time from achievement
paragraphs: The daily 30 minutes is a planning guide, not a measured guarantee of mastery within that time. If unfinished, record what is established and what remains, then prioritize the next practice.

Do not mark an item as fully checked in both explanation and practical performance merely because you have read it. An app score or a single correction does not certify overall care skills, professional approval or a pass in the official examination.

kaigo-review-05-knowledge-3.heading: Today’s review situation
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Review two submitted practice questions using a fictional review sheet. Correct the assumption that a dish on the table proves the person used it. This does not represent a learner’s actual score or care abilities.

kaigo-review-05-words.heading: Vocabulary and useful expressions
paragraphs: 確認（かくにん） — Checking: clarifying uncertainty by asking or observing directly.
内容（ないよう） — Content: matters contained in speech or writing.
記録（きろく） — Recording: preserving confirmed conditions, assistance and responses with dates and times.
未確認（みかくにん） — Unconfirmed: not yet checked; it does not mean no problem exists.
食器（しょっき） — Tableware: bowls, plates and similar items used for food or at the table.
報告（ほうこく） — Report: specifically communicating observations and actions to the necessary recipient.
Useful expression: The dish’s location is confirmed, but its use by the person is not. I’ll separate an object’s state from the person’s action.
Useful expression: I’ll record today’s explained distinction separately from the next practice task. One correction does not establish mastery of all care skills or passing the official examination.

kaigo-review-05-dialogue.heading: Discuss errors and further practice
paragraphs: [Situation created for learning] Review two submitted practice questions using a fictional review sheet. Correct the assumption that a dish on the table proves the person used it. This does not represent a learner’s actual score or care abilities.
Naoto Kawase: Let’s review the submitted sheet. How would you correct concluding that the person used a dish because it was on the table?
Care worker Tanaka: The dish’s location is confirmed, but its use by the person is not. I’ll separate an object’s state from the person’s action.
Naoto Kawase: Apart from memorizing an option number, what will you practice to avoid this error?
Care worker Tanaka: I’ll mark the subject and confirmed information, write one unconfirmed action and explain the same distinction in another situation.
Naoto Kawase: Let’s practice that one type today and leave the rest for next time. How will you record achievement?
Care worker Tanaka: I’ll record today’s explained distinction separately from the next practice task. One correction does not establish mastery of all care skills or passing the official examination.

kaigo-review-05-transfer-legacy.heading: Check understanding in another situation
paragraphs: [Learning example] A towel was prepared beside the washbasin, but whether the person washed their face is unconfirmed.

We know that the towel has been prepared. Before recording that the person has finished washing their face, separately confirm what they actually did. Distinguish the state of the prepared items from the person’s actions.
Example wording: “I have prepared the towel. I have not yet confirmed whether the person has finished washing their face. I will check what has been done with the person responsible.”
Review: Explain confirmed facts, unknowns, who to ask and what to check. Apply the distinction to other objects and actions rather than memorizing only the dish example.

kaigo-review-05-reading.heading: Read a practice review sheet
paragraphs:
Review sheet after submission
Today’s task: Distinguish object states from personal actions. Practice record: ‘The dish is on the table’ is confirmed. ‘The person used it’ is unconfirmed. Next time: Explain another example where preparation differs from implementation. This fictional sheet is not an examinee’s actual score.

kaigo-language-transfer-266.heading: Separate event records from assumed causes
paragraphs: At 8:10, a comb was dropped on the floor. Who had been using it is unconfirmed. The responsible person will check its condition.
Check: The time and comb-dropping event are recorded. The user is unconfirmed, and the responsible person will check the condition next.
Approach: Do not invent an omitted subject and conclude that the person used it or was careless. Separate the recorded event, unknown identity and planned checking.

kaigo-atomic-stress.heading: Emotions, motivation and stressors
paragraphs: People experience and express joy, anger, sadness and enjoyment differently. The same situation does not necessarily produce identical feelings. Expressions and behavior offer clues, but check the person’s own words rather than concluding emotions from them alone.
Motivation means feeling a personal wish to do something. Support meaningful goals and choice rather than assuming staff should take over actions the person can do.

Stressors include physical environmental factors such as noise and temperature, bodily factors such as fatigue, poor sleep or hunger, and psychological or social factors such as anxiety, fear, excitement and relationships. Tension can appear in the body as well as the mind.

Life history, education and age-related experiences influence thinking and expression, but do not establish what this person thinks. Do not attribute distress to personality; check habits, surroundings and condition.

[Learning example] Recording ‘dislikes socializing’ when the person says the room is noisy changes the meaning. Preserve the statement about sound and ask whether they want a quieter place or a break.

This section teaches concepts and reasons for observation. Actual assistance and measurement follow personal condition, the individual care plan, equipment instructions and facility training. Do not record guessed values or diagnoses.

kaigo-atomic-memory.heading: Distinguish memory processes and types
paragraphs: Encoding means learning new experiences, retention means keeping the information and recall means retrieving it when needed. Difficulty remembering does not necessarily reflect the same problem at every stage.

Short-term memory retains information briefly; long-term memory keeps it longer. Long-term types include episodic memory for specific experiences and semantic memory for knowledge such as word meanings.
Procedural memory involves learned movements and skills. Priming means previous exposure influences later responses, sometimes without conscious recall. Do not merge these types into one ability.

[Learning example] A person may be able to use familiar scissors but have difficulty remembering a schedule they have just heard. This is not necessarily a contradiction. One retained skill does not show that all memory is preserved. Record what the person can do separately from their difficulties and arrange the necessary assessment.

This section teaches concepts and reasons for observation. Actual assistance and measurement follow personal condition, the individual care plan, equipment instructions and facility training. Do not record guessed values or diagnoses.

kaigo-atomic-needs.heading: Use needs categories to understand personal life
paragraphs: Needs are feelings of wanting something or wanting to do something. Maslow’s model distinguishes five: physiological needs such as food, drink and sleep; safety; belonging and love through relationships; esteem through recognition; and self-actualization through fulfilling one’s abilities.
The textbook groups physiology and safety as basic needs and connection, esteem and self-actualization as social needs. Connection with others and recognition of personal worth also differ.

These categories help explore wishes from several perspectives. People needing physical help also want relationships and meaningful activities. Do not use the model as a step-by-step completion procedure or a ranking of human worth.
[Learning example] Needing help eating does not justify ignoring a wish to see friends. Check eating assistance and safety while also asking about relationships and personal choices.

This section teaches concepts and reasons for observation. Actual assistance and measurement follow personal condition, the individual care plan, equipment instructions and facility training. Do not record guessed values or diagnoses.

kaigo-atomic-temperature.heading: Homeostasis, daily variation and temperature conditions
paragraphs: Homeostasis keeps internal conditions within a range despite environmental change. Losing heat through sweating when hot is one example. It does not mean one identical value is maintained under every circumstance.

Body temperature varies across the day and between people. The textbook describes a tendency to be higher during daytime and lower during nighttime sleep. Consider actual routines, activity and health and compare with the person’s usual condition.

The textbook’s armpit example places the thermometer tip appropriately in the armpit and closes the arm to hold it. Its hemiplegia example uses the unaffected side. Actual measurement follows the plan, device instructions and training without forcing posture.

Ear and forehead devices also exist, but sites and technologies differ. Record time, value and unit, site, device and conditions. Do not treat ear and armpit values as two measurements under identical conditions.

Temperature, respiration, pulse and blood pressure provide vital-sign information about condition and change. Do not judge overall health from one value alone. Consider personal concerns and differences from usual and tell the appropriate recipient about changes.

This section teaches concepts and reasons for observation. Actual assistance and measurement follow personal condition, the individual care plan, equipment instructions and facility training. Do not record guessed values or diagnoses.

kaigo-atomic-breathing.heading: Airways, gas exchange and respiratory observation
paragraphs: The airway is the passage for air, including nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, trachea and bronchi. Gas exchange occurs between lung alveoli and surrounding blood: oxygen enters blood, and carbon dioxide leaves blood through the lungs and out of the body.

Breathing is usually regulated without conscious effort, but varies with age, activity, feelings, health and disease. Observe not only frequency but breathlessness, breathing effort, sounds, sputum and differences from usual.

Bluish-purple coloring of the lips or nails, called cyanosis, is an important change that may be associated with insufficient oxygen. However, the absence of this color change does not establish that the person is safe. Promptly seek assessment by a healthcare professional for new breathlessness. In an emergency, such as severe breathing difficulty, immediately seek help according to the facility’s emergency procedures.

Cough and sputum help remove foreign material and other substances from airways. Report observations such as persistent cough or changed sputum color. Observation alone does not determine a pathogen or disease.

This section teaches concepts and reasons for observation. Actual assistance and measurement follow personal condition, the individual care plan, equipment instructions and facility training. Do not record guessed values or diagnoses.

kaigo-atomic-pulse.heading: Pulse sites and observation conditions
paragraphs: Pulse is the change felt as heartbeats travel through arteries. Check rhythm and strength as well as frequency. Report actual measured values and observations with time, site, method and condition.

The textbook figures identify the radial artery at the wrist, brachial artery near the elbow, superficial temporal artery at the side of the head and carotid artery in the neck. Sites also exist at the groin and top of the foot. Identifying names does not authorize independent manipulation, especially around the neck.

Pulse varies with age, activity, tension, health and illness. Children tend to have faster pulses than adults, but do not assume every person’s pulse slows identically with age. Check individual factors such as medication with healthcare professionals and consider usual condition and measurement conditions.

[Learning example] ‘Pulse normal’ alone does not communicate measured frequency, rhythm, site or time. Give actual measurements specifically; do not invent unmeasured numbers, which remain unconfirmed.

This section teaches concepts and reasons for observation. Actual assistance and measurement follow personal condition, the individual care plan, equipment instructions and facility training. Do not record guessed values or diagnoses.

58.title: Understand emotions, motivation and stress
objectives: Check personal feelings through expressions and words.
Distinguish environmental, bodily and psychosocial stressors.
58.context: Practice checking words and wishes when a person says the gathering room is noisy, without assuming personality or social preferences.
58.artCaption: Listen to the person’s words and important experiences and check feelings without assuming them.

59.title: Distinguish memory processes and types
objectives: Do not infer that one preserved memory or skill establishes other memory abilities.
59.context: Consider someone who can perform a familiar manual task but cannot recall a new schedule. This learning example distinguishes functions; it is not a diagnosis.
59.artCaption: Check familiar hand movements separately from remembering experiences and schedules.

60.title: Consider bodily and social needs
objectives: Connect Maslow’s five needs with specific examples.
Respect relationships and personal choices even when physical assistance is needed.
60.context: Practice avoiding the assumption that eating assistance makes asking about seeing friends unnecessary. Do not use needs categories to rank personal worth.
60.artCaption: Choosing flowers can involve enjoyment, relationships and personal choice.

61.title: Understand homeostasis and temperature measurement conditions
objectives: Explain homeostasis, daily variation and individual differences.
Record time, site, device and condition as well as values.
61.context: Consider whether ear and armpit temperatures are measurements under identical conditions. This learning example does not assess a particular person’s illness.
61.artCaption: Check measurement conditions while talking with the person. The depicted device alone does not establish the temperature method or result.

62.title: Observe the breathing pathway and changes
objectives: Explain airways and gas exchange in the lungs.
Report distress, sounds, sputum and differences from usual as well as frequency.
62.context: Review the mistaken idea of waiting for lip-color changes when new breathlessness appears. This is not independent diagnosis or specification of treatment.
62.artCaption: Listen and observe breathing. A clock on the desk alone does not establish completed measurement.

63.title: Report pulse observations and actual measurements
objectives: Distinguish pulse frequency, rhythm, strength and measurement sites.
Report actual information rather than only age or the word normal.
63.context: Consider a handoff saying only ‘pulse normal.’ Do not add unmeasured values; clarify what was established.
63.artCaption: Consult nursing staff, distinguishing the person’s own words, observations and actual measurements.

kaigo-review-05.title: Explain errors and decide the next practice
objectives: Separate confirmed facts from assumptions and explain errors in your own words.
Check understanding with a new example and carry unfinished tasks into further learning.
kaigo-review-05.context: Review two submitted practice questions using a fictional sheet, correcting the inference that a dish on the table proves personal use. This does not represent actual scores or care ability.
kaigo-review-05.artCaption: Staff review a meal example, separating prepared items from what the person actually did.

options: The person used the dish.
The dish is on the table.
The meal is finished.
Assistance is complete.
rationales: A confirmed location alone does not prove the person used the dish.
The review sheet identifies its location on the table as confirmed.
Completed eating is not established by this review sheet.
Completed assistance is not stated and cannot be inferred from the dish’s location.
weekly-review-q21.reading:
Review sheet after submission
Today’s task: Distinguish object states from personal actions. Practice record: ‘The dish is on the table’ is confirmed. ‘The person used it’ is unconfirmed. Next time: Explain another example where preparation differs from implementation. This fictional sheet is not an examinee’s actual score.

weekly-review-q22.prompt: You inferred that the person used the dish because it was on the table. What is the main error?
options: Only assuming the person cannot read.
Only forgetting the answer number.
Writing the same dish name twice.
Inferring personal action from an object’s state.
rationales: This case concerns inference beyond the evidence, not a judgment of reading ability.
The problem is confusing fact types, not remembering an option number.
Nothing identifies the number of written dish names as an error.
The object’s presence has been substituted for the person’s action of using it.
weekly-review-q22.reading:
Review sheet after submission
Today’s task: Distinguish object states from personal actions. Practice record: ‘The dish is on the table’ is confirmed. ‘The person used it’ is unconfirmed. Next time: Explain another example where preparation differs from implementation. This fictional sheet is not an examinee’s actual score.

options: Identify the subject and confirmed scope and explain another example.
Mark every unknown field complete.
Memorize the same sentence without another example.
Repeat only the correct option number.
rationales: Identifying the subject and evidence scope and explaining another case checks understanding.
This changes records without correcting the error.
Memorization alone does not check application to a different situation.
An option number alone does not show why the error occurred.
weekly-review-q23.reading:
Review sheet after submission
Today’s task: Distinguish object states from personal actions. Practice record: ‘The dish is on the table’ is confirmed. ‘The person used it’ is unconfirmed. Next time: Explain another example where preparation differs from implementation. This fictional sheet is not an examinee’s actual score.

weekly-review-q24.prompt: What does this review sheet show?
options: An actual total score.
Official proof of passing.
A fictional task and next practice plan.
Certification of all care skills.
rationales: No actual total score appears on the sheet.
It is not an official passing certificate.
The text explains that it shows a fictional task and further practice.
Reviewing one reading task does not certify all care skills.
weekly-review-q24.reading:
Review sheet after submission
Today’s task: Distinguish object states from personal actions. Practice record: ‘The dish is on the table’ is confirmed. ‘The person used it’ is unconfirmed. Next time: Explain another example where preparation differs from implementation. This fictional sheet is not an examinee’s actual score.

weekly-review-q25.prompt: What cannot be established from a prepared towel alone?
options: Completed face washing by the person.
That a towel was prepared.
That a towel exists.
That the record concerns a prepared item.
rationales: Preparation alone does not establish completed face washing.
Preparation is an established condition of this question.
The preparation condition establishes that a towel is present.
The question clearly concerns a prepared item.
weekly-review-q25.reading:
Review sheet after submission
Today’s task: Distinguish object states from personal actions. Practice record: ‘The dish is on the table’ is confirmed. ‘The person used it’ is unconfirmed. Next time: Explain another example where preparation differs from implementation. This fictional sheet is not an examinee’s actual score.

weekly-kaigo-knowledge-56-1.prompt: Which method is appropriate for reviewing an incorrect answer?
options: Copy only the correct number without checking reasons.
Identify the error and supporting correction evidence and explain the same idea in another example.
Record every unsolved question as complete.
Repeat only the original sentence without other situations.
rationales: A number alone does not explain which knowledge or condition was misunderstood.
This organizes the reason and checks application to a new situation.
The record would not match actual achievement and would hide remaining tasks.
Memorizing the original alone does not test understanding under other conditions.

weekly-kaigo-knowledge-56-2.prompt: You correctly read a transfer sequence. What is appropriate regarding practical skills?
options: Check operation, coordination with the person and safety under instruction; practical competence is not yet established.
Reading permits trying alone despite no experience.
A correct answer removes the need to check the individual care plan.
Record practical assessment complete and omit instructor checks.
rationales: Reading sequence knowledge differs from skill using appropriate force and position, which needs separate checking.
Reading success does not replace equipment, staffing or practical-ability checks.
A text question differs from the real person’s conditions; the individual care plan still needs checking.
An assessment not yet performed cannot be recorded as verified.

weekly-kaigo-language-transfer-266.prompt: Which pair correctly identifies established and unknown information?
options: The person’s carelessness is confirmed as the dropping cause.
The responsible person already finished checking.
A comb was dropped at 8:10; who had used it is unknown.
Unknown identity means no time is recorded.
rationales: With the user unknown, neither personal identity nor cause can be invented.
‘Will check’ refers to a future action, not completion.
This separates the recorded event from the explicitly unknown identity.
The user is unknown, but 8:10 is written.
weekly-kaigo-language-transfer-266.reading: At 8:10, a comb was dropped on the floor. Who had been using it is unconfirmed. The responsible person will check its condition.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-stress.prompt: The person says the gathering room is noisy. Which record is appropriate?
options: Conclude they dislike socializing by personality.
Record the statement about noise and ask about wishes such as a quieter place.
Record refusal of every future activity.
Write that they enjoy the noise based only on expression.
rationales: Discomfort with noise does not establish general social preferences or personality.
This respects the environmental statement without replacing it with personality assumptions.
This room’s noise concern does not establish blanket refusal.
Staff assumptions contradict the person’s explicit words.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-memory.prompt: The person uses familiar scissors but cannot recall a newly heard schedule. Which understanding is appropriate?
options: Scissor use proves the schedule is remembered.
Failure to recall means no manual tasks are possible.
These conflict, so omit the person’s account.
Check familiar skills and remembering new plans as different aspects of memory.
rationales: Procedural skill alone does not establish encoding or recall of new information.
This generalizes one difficulty to an actually preserved skill.
Different functions need not match; record each rather than treating them as contradictory.
One skill does not establish that every memory process is preserved.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-needs.prompt: Someone says a person needing eating assistance need not be asked about seeing friends. What understanding is missing?
options: Physical help means social needs disappear.
Staff selecting friends removes personal choice.
Relationship and choice wishes still need checking despite physical support needs.
Needs categories rank human worth.
rationales: Physical assistance needs do not establish absence of relationship wishes.
Respect personal wishes rather than deciding relationships for them.
Support physiological needs and wishes for social connection together.
The model helps understand life; it does not rank people’s value.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-temperature.prompt: Ear and armpit temperatures were compared and reported only as ‘higher.’ What information is needed?
options: Values and units, times, sites, devices and conditions, distinguishing the different measurement conditions.
Different values always prove fever despite different sites.
Invent the usual value if the previous value is unknown.
Age alone is enough; measurement conditions are unnecessary.
rationales: Preserving site and method differences helps the recipient understand comparison conditions.
A difference alone does not establish fever without checking conditions and the usual pattern.
Invented unmeasured values are not factual records.
Age alone does not communicate actual values or comparison conditions.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-breathing.prompt: New breathlessness occurs without bluish-purple lips. Which approach is appropriate?
options: Wait to report until lip color changes.
Count breaths only, ignoring distress and usual differences.
Diagnose an emotional cause because lips are unchanged.
Seek help promptly without waiting for color changes and follow emergency procedures for severe difficulty or other urgent conditions.
rationales: No color change does not justify leaving breathlessness unaddressed.
Personal concerns, breathing appearance and sounds also need observation.
Color alone does not establish the cause.
Breathlessness itself is important; cyanosis is not a prerequisite for seeking help.

weekly-kaigo-atomic-case-pulse.prompt: A handoff says only ‘pulse normal.’ What information should be communicated?
options: An age-appropriate guess even without measuring.
Confirmed measured frequency and unit, time, site, regularity and strength.
Frequency alone, omitting every time and condition.
One normal observation removes the need to check later changes.
rationales: Do not record guessed values that were not measured.
Use a record showing actual measurements and observation scope rather than an impression alone.
Timing and conditions help the recipient understand changes.
One observation does not prove future stability.
